activities.anchor: That sounds negligibly slow until you run it
activities.caption: fill the blanks — the three joints of the map
activities.name: ptBoundaryCloze

config.text: Plates spread apart at %%0%%, dive under each other at %%1%%, and grind past one another at %%2%% — moving 2 to 10 cm a year, about as fast as fingernails grow.
config.hint: One builds crust, one destroys it, one does neither.

activities.caption: bet before you read on — the solid-rock verdict
activities.name: ptSwavePredict

config.q: S-waves cannot travel through liquid — yet they arrive straight through the mantle beneath your feet. What does that prove?
choices: The mantle is a sea of liquid magma that plates float on
The mantle is almost entirely solid rock
S-waves are slower underground than in the crust
config.why: The old picture of plates as crustal rafts on molten rock fails: the asthenosphere is solid rock — hot enough to flow over aeons, rigid enough to carry shear waves on every human timescale.

activities.caption: file each item: evidence, or mechanism
activities.name: ptMoralBuckets

config.prompt: A theory needs both evidence and mechanism. In the drift story, which is which?

items.label: matching coastlines on either side of the Atlantic
magnetic stripes symmetrical about every ridge

config.why: Wegener had the evidence in 1912 and was ignored because he lacked the mechanism; Hess's 1962 conveyor supplied it, and Vine and Matthews' 1963 stripes clinched the pair together. A theory without a mechanism is a story; evidence without a theory is trivia.

activities.anchor: a field trip to the seam of the world
activities.caption: pair each landscape with its boundary
activities.name: ptBoundaryMatch

config.prompt: Three boundary types, one planet — pair the place with the boundary that built it:

pairs.right: divergent — a continent visibly beginning to split
divergent — a ridge fortuitously above sea level
convergent — ocean floor sliding beneath South America
convergent — continent on continent, still raising Everest

pairs.left: the longest mountain chain on Earth
pairs.right: divergent — the mid-ocean ridge system, mostly underwater and unvisited

config.why: Divergent boundaries build ridges and rift valleys; convergent ones build trenches, volcanic arcs and fold mountains. Splitting one continent apart can look like three different geographies.

activities.caption: pin the depth — the only deep quakes
activities.name: ptDeepPlace

config.prompt: Subduction zones host the only deep earthquakes. How far down the slab do they descend?
config.why: About 700 km — the subducted slab quaking as it warms, on inclined Wadati–Benioff planes no other boundary can reach.

activities.caption: find the faulty line — the seismology brief
activities.name: ptSeismoSpot

config.prompt: One line of this seismology brief is wrong — click it:
lines: Friction locks the fault while rock bends and stores strain like a compressed spring.
The stored strain releases in seconds as seismic waves.
P-waves arrive first, S-waves second, surface waves last.
The epicentre is the point of rupture underground.
Each whole magnitude step is about 32 times the energy.
config.correction: The point of rupture underground is the focus; the epicentre is the point directly above it.
config.why: Arrival-time differences locate the source and wave heights size the event — but underground rupture is the focus, and the epicentre is only its overhead projection.

activities.caption: drag the divider — runny versus sticky
activities.name: ptMagmaCompare

config.prompt: The same mountain-building force, two personalities — drag the divider:

before.label: basaltic — silica-poor
before.text: Hot, runny, lets gas escape easily — erupts gently and flows far, building Hawaii's broad shield volcanoes. Kīlauea has erupted almost continuously for decades, and tourists watch from marked paths.

after.label: andesitic-to-rhyolitic — silica-rich
after.text: Cooler, sticky, traps its gas until the pressure is catastrophic — then explodes into steep composite cones: St Helens 1980, Krakatoa 1883, and the calderas of super-eruptions like Yellowstone.

config.why: The decisive variable is silica content and the gas it traps — which is also why Pinatubo 1991 cooled the planet about half a degree while Kīlauea never has.

activities.anchor: ran up to 40 m on steep coasts
activities.caption: call the magnitude — the inundation
activities.name: ptTsunamiEstimate

config.prompt: Tōhoku 2011: the tsunami overtopped 10 m sea walls. How far inland did it flood across the plain, in km²?
config.why: About 560 km² of Japan was flooded — the sea, not the shaking, was the killer, and it knocked out Fukushima's cooling on the way in.
config.context: Waves reached 40 m on steep coasts and nearly 20,000 people died — Japan's engineered buildings, by contrast, mostly stood.
